messages.content: You identify plain-language Discussion Units in a legal decision. Use only the supplied numbered paragraphs. Group contiguous paragraphs that perform one coherent task, such as procedural history, facts, party submissions, legal test, analysis/application, or disposition. Do not invent facts or citations. Return JSON with a units array. Each unit must contain start_paragraph, end_paragraph, label, explanation, transition_from_previous, and confidence. Use paragraph indices exactly as supplied; never output an index not present in the supplied list, and cover the supplied window from its first index through its last index exactly once. Keep explanations short and readable for a legal researcher.

{"case_id": 7948, "contract_version": "discussion_units_llm_v1", "deterministic_baseline": {"discussion_unit_count": 2, "units": [{"end_paragraph": 5, "generation_method": "discussion_unit_v1", "start_paragraph": 0}, {"end_paragraph": 7, "generation_method": "discussion_unit_v1", "start_paragraph": 6}]}, "paragraph_window": {"first_allowed": 1, "last_allowed": 5}, "paragraphs": [{"citation_ids": [], "container_paragraph_index": 1, "is_heading": false, "paragraph_index": 1, "source_paragraph_index": 1, "statute_ids": [], "tag_ids": [], "text": "[1] Mr. Grillo is a citizen of Italy. On October 1, 2019, he entered Canada as a visitor. Proceedings were commenced against him to have him declared inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality, because he pleaded guilty to a drug-related offence in the United States and was sentenced to 10 years in prison. For this reason, the Immigration Division [ID] of the Immigration and Refugee Board declared him inadmissible on November 7, 2019, under paragraph 36(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA]. Mr. Grillo is now seeking judicial review of this decision."}, {"citation_ids": [], "container_paragraph_index": 2, "is_heading": false, "paragraph_index": 2, "source_paragraph_index": 2, "statute_ids": [], "tag_ids": [], "text": "[2] The role of the Court on judicial review is to ensure that the decision under review is reasonable. Specifically, this means that the decision must be assessed on the basis of the evidence and arguments that were before the decision maker. Judicial review is not an opportunity to raise new arguments. However, this is precisely what Mr. Grillo is attempting to do. The arguments that he is now raising were not put before the ID. They are therefore inadmissible. They cannot be used as a basis for a finding that the ID\u2019s decision is unreasonable. I will nevertheless address them briefly to demonstrate that they are entirely devoid of merit."}, {"citation_ids": [], "container_paragraph_index": 3, "is_heading": false, "paragraph_index": 3, "source_paragraph_index": 3, "statute_ids": [], "tag_ids": [], "text": "[3] Mr. Grillo\u2019s first argument concerns the equivalence between the American offence and the Canadian offence. Mr. Grillo submits that the ID should have performed a detailed comparison of the essential elements of each offence and its potential defences. However, if the ID addressed this point only briefly, it is because at his hearing before the ID, Mr. Grillo did not challenge the equivalence between the two offences. In addition, even before this Court, Mr. Grillo does not explain how the American and Canadian offences differ. It is hardly surprising that conspiring to traffic in cocaine constitutes a criminal offence in both countries. I note that the ID was not required to retry the American case or speculate on the chance of success of certain defences, given that Mr. Grillo in fact pleaded guilty. Mr. Grillo has therefore failed to establish that the ID\u2019s decision is unreasonable."}, {"citation_ids": [], "container_paragraph_index": 4, "is_heading": false, "paragraph_index": 4, "source_paragraph_index": 4, "statute_ids": [], "tag_ids": [], "text": "[4] Mr. Grillo\u2019s second argument concerns the report prepared under section 44 of the IRPA, which commenced the proceedings before the ID. In his view, the description of the Canadian offence in the report is inadequate because it does not refer to the relevant paragraph of subsection 465(1) of the Criminal Code and because it does not specify that the substance was cocaine. To accept such arguments would be excessively formalistic. Mr. Grillo cannot seriously claim to have suffered any prejudice on account of the failure to mention these details. There is no room for doubt regarding the conviction on which his inadmissibility was based or the nature of the substance at issue."}, {"citation_ids": [], "container_paragraph_index": 5, "is_heading": false, "paragraph_index": 5, "source_paragraph_index": 5, "statute_ids": [], "tag_ids": [], "text": "[5] For these reasons, the application for judicial review will be dismissed."}], "request_id": "discussion-units-case-7948"}

units.label: Procedural History
units.explanation: Introduces Mr. Grillo's background, the inadmissibility decision, and the judicial review sought.

units.label: Legal Standard for Judicial Review
units.explanation: Explains the court's role to assess reasonableness based on the record and the inadmissibility of new arguments.

units.label: Analysis of the First Argument (Offence Equivalence)
units.explanation: Addresses Mr. Grillo's claim about offence comparison, noting he did not challenge this before the ID and failed to demonstrate differences.

units.label: Analysis of the Second Argument (Report Description)
units.explanation: Evaluates Mr. Grillo's complaint about the report's adequacy, concluding lack of prejudice and sufficiency of the evidence.
units.transition_from_previous: Analysis of the First Argument (Offence Equivalence)

units.label: Disposition
units.explanation: States the court's decision to dismiss the application for judicial review based on the previous reasoning.
units.transition_from_previous: Analysis of the Second Argument (Report Description)
